Every other project assessed on 2026-10-06/07 pooled: three plants per leaf replicate (Danilevskaya), up to 32 ears per plot (same), five heads per pot (FHB), five leaf discs from five plants (Range 28), five leaves per pot (Russ), ten seeds (PGRC). So this is the one cohort where a co-detection of two fungi is evidence about one PLANT rather than one plot. Worth knowing when the co-infection network is built: it is the natural place to check whether plot-level pooling inflates apparent co-occurrence

value: PRJEB8798 mixes in-planta samples with axenic broth cultures, and scientific_name splits it wrongly
note: 21 of 51 runs are registered as Zymoseptoria tritici IPO323 and 30 as Triticum aestivum, which looks like the in-vitro/in-planta split and is not: only 6 of the 21 are broth cultures (CDB x3, PDB x3), the other 15 being the same infected wheat leaves registered under the pathogen. The usable key is the ENA sample_title, which is explicit ('Z.tritici on wheat leafs (9dpi)' versus 'Z.tritici grown on potato dextrose broth (PDB)'). A general warning for dual RNA-seq deposits: the registered organism tells you which side the submitter was interested in, not whether a plant was present

value: PRJNA718488 is a documented field CO-INFECTION: leaf rust by design, powdery mildew by accident
note: 'Nearby, in two parallel rows, a large experiment with powdery mildew was performed FROM WHICH OUR EXPERIMENTAL PLANTS WERE ALSO INFECTED.' So the 15 infected flag leaves carry Puccinia triticina AND Blumeria graminis, both reported by the authors. Two uses. First, it is a positive control for the whole method: if the pipeline cannot recover two reported pathogens from these 15 runs, it will not find an unreported third anywhere. Second, the 15 CONTROL plants grew 400 m away in the same field during a deliberate rust epidemic plus an adjacent mildew experiment, which makes them an unusually sharp test of cryptic infection in nominally healthy field tissue

value: Archive metadata can EXCLUDE a project but not ADMIT one - the working asymmetry
note: Leon's no-manuscript-no-entry policy says a deposit without an available manuscript does not enter the cohort however good its metadata. It says nothing against using metadata to rule a project OUT, and the risk is asymmetric: a wrongly excluded field project is a loss we can detect later by re-reading, while a wrongly admitted one silently corrupts a rate. So the BioProject Description and the GEO growth protocol are now the FIRST filter, and papers are hunted only for projects that still look field. Nine projects and 759 runs were cleared this way in one pass. The evidence rows say plainly which source each quote came from, so any of them can be upgraded to a methods section later

value: How the STAT-frame runs get assessed: the archive-first procedure, unchanged
note: 1. Import the projects into the literature frame via seeds/backfill_accessions.tsv then triage, so they gain runinfo plus BioSample attributes and enter the audit chain. 2. value: BioProject Descriptions are nearly useless for STAT-frame projects: 74 of 81 give no signal

Literature-frame projects arrived largely as GEO deposits, and GEO forces a Description and a per-sample growth protocol; these are ENA/SRA direct submissions whose Description is often boilerplate - 'Sequencing reads associated with the study: Comparative genomics of brown rust field samples' is the WHOLE record. So for this frame the cheap bulk source is not the BioProject Description but the BIOSAMPLE ATTRIBUTES and the ENA report, which carry geo_loc_name, collection_date and tissue per sample - the barley backfill gained 270 locations, 121 dates and 346 tissues that way. value: PRJEB65589 RESOLVED by Notes S1: field pathogenomics, 53 runs, all field
note: The Viewpoints article carries no methods; Notes S1 does. RNA was extracted directly from the leaves or stems of Pgt-infected bread wheat collected in the UK, Germany, France, Uganda and South Africa, with no increase step before sequencing. The controlled work in Notes S1 section 3 is a separate virulence assay: spores harvested from the 20 UK 2022 samples, multiplied on susceptible cv. Vuka under 16-h light at 18/12 C, for phenotyping only. Two lessons. First, a Viewpoints or Perspective piece can still own a primary deposit, with its methods banished to Supporting Information; do not read 'no methods in the article' as 'no methods available'. Second, this is the strongest argument yet for the linked-sentence rule: both a field extraction and a controlled multiplication appear in the same four-page supplement, and only the sentence containing the RNA extraction describes the sequenced material.

value: The kraken read-based host call disagrees with the curated host for 76 of 1,299 runs, and the error is one-directional
note: Leon asked why the 03_kraken charts show barley co-infections when the curated field cereal cohort has almost no barley. Answer: most of that barley is not barley. Kraken calls Hordeum vulgare for 141 runs; of the 35 that carry a field setting, the papers' own per-sample tables say otherwise, and Ada21 settles it - for the 20 of those runs that ada21_runs.csv curates, Table S1 says Triticum aestivum 18 and Secale cereale 2, and barley 0. Genus agreement overall is 94% (1,223/1,299), but the disagreement is ASYMMETRIC: 32 runs called Hordeum that are curated Triticum, and ZERO called Triticum that are curated Hordeum. A symmetric error would be noise; one direction is a bias. Twenty-one further runs are called Ipomoea (sweet potato) and are all curated wheat. Every misassigned run is in a rust survey - PRJEB39201, PRJEB36485, PRJEB65589, PRJEB31334, PRJEB47693, PRJNA950118 - and the mechanism shows in the read fractions: misassigned runs have a median host_pct of 8.25 against 19.03 where the call agrees. These are field-pathogenomics libraries where the fungus dominates and the plant is a minority of reads, so the host call is made on thin evidence and drifts, within Triticeae for the Hordeum case and further for Ipomoea. Consequence: where a curated host exists it should outrank the read-based call in any downstream grouping, and a host call on a library with a low host fraction should be treated as a flag rather than a fact. The barley gap is real; it is not a curation error.

value: Crop is almost perfectly confounded with sampling_selection in the field cereal cohort, so a crop comparison is not estimable
note: Field cereal samples by crop and selection: wheat 1,200/1,251 disease-selected (96%); rice 2,784/2,784 unselected (100%); sorghum 1,119/1,120 unselected (100%); maize 2,287/2,511 unselected (91%). There is no disease-selected rice, sorghum or maize to speak of, and almost no unselected wheat. The strata do not overlap, so no model can separate 'wheat has more co-infection' from 'disease-selected samples have more co-infection' - they are the same 1,200 samples. This is not a confounder to adjust for; it is a design separation. It also means the locality disparity (wheat 353 localities, rice 6) is a symptom rather than the problem: wheat is broad because rust surveys sample broadly, rice is deep because GWAS panels sit at one farm. The consequence is that the two evidence standards are the only honest framing - wheat answers 'is there a SECOND pathogen in known-infected plants', rice/maize/sorghum answer 'is there a FIRST unreported pathogen in unselected plants' - and those are two findings, not two arms of one comparison.

value: The field cereal co-infection rate moves from 99% to 57% on the coverage threshold alone
note: Measured 2026-10-09 over 1,210 classified field cereal runs. Counting every row of _classified.tsv gives a 100% co-infection rate, which is wrong twice over: the file holds three cls values and only 'real' is a detection (real 12,092, crash-out 8,993, unclassified 3,382). Restricting to cls=real still gives 99% of runs with 2+ species and a mean of 6.00 species per run. Adding coverage >=0.1% gives 88% and 4.16; coverage >=1% gives 57% and 2.08, with the per-project rate spanning 0 to 100% and a median of 55%. So the headline number is set by the threshold, not by the data, and nothing in the cohort itself says which threshold is right. That is the argument for the negative controls. One thing that is NOT a confounder: sequencing depth. Spearman between log10 depth and species count at 1% coverage is +0.05 overall, and within-project rho scatters from -0.36 to +0.28 with no consistent sign, because coverage is a fraction of k-mer space and is already depth-normalised.

value: A locality that resolves only at its last ladder rung is a COUNTRY placement, and was being drawn as a locality circle
note: Three separate faults, found because Leon asked why a wheat point sat in the middle of Australia. (1) The query ladder ends with the bare country, so a locality that fails every finer rung still 'succeeds' - at the country centroid - and was labelled by the rung INDEX rather than by what it is. 61 named localities and 267 samples were placed at a country centroid while drawn as locality circles, which is the exact misrepresentation the diamond convention exists to prevent, except invisible. Fixed by labelling the rung 'country' whenever the query that answered is the country itself. (2) 158 runs across 12 strings carried a DOUBLED country prefix from the 2026-10-02 BioSample import - 'China: China:Anyang', 'France: France: Blanquefort', 'Australia: Australia: Canberra' - and Nominatim returns nothing for the doubled form, so all of them fell back silently. (3) Cleaning the location string must apply to the QUERY only: rewriting the stored key unjoined every corrected locality from prep_crop_map.py, which looks rows up by the string as curated, and sent them straight back to country centroids. Net recovery 267 -> 229 samples at country precision, and the remaining 229 are now honestly drawn as diamonds.
